title: What the Election Assistance Commission Does — and Why Its Independence Matters
hook: A little-known federal commission certifies voting machines and helps run U.S. elections. In 2026 the president removed its last sitting members, months before the midterms.
key_points: The U.S. Election Assistance Commission (EAC) was created after the 2000 Florida recount to help states run elections and to test and certify voting equipment.
By design it's bipartisan: up to four commissioners, no more than two from one party, meant to insulate election administration from any single party's control.
In July 2026 the president removed the commission's remaining members, leaving it without its statutory leadership ahead of the midterms.
Election administration is otherwise run by the states — the EAC has no power to run elections itself, only to set voluntary standards and support local officials.
The episode raises the same question as other fights over independent agencies: how much protection from at-will removal can a body Congress designed as bipartisan actually keep?
content_html: Most voters have never heard of the U.S. Election Assistance Commission, and that's by design — it doesn't run elections. Congress created it after the chaotic 2000 Florida recount to do something narrower but important: test and certify voting machines, and give state and local election officials federal money and technical support. To keep it out of partisan hands, the law caps it at four commissioners with no more than two from either party.
extra_html: In July 2026, President Trump removed the commission's remaining members, according to reporting from ProPublica's Jen Fifield and NPR's Benjamin Swasey — leaving the EAC without its statutory leadership just months before the midterms, a move Democrats and voting-rights advocates condemned. The move doesn't change who runs elections day to day — that job stays with the states — but it does test how much insulation a body Congress designed to be genuinely bipartisan can hold onto, a version of the same removal-power question playing out across other independent agencies. One of the three, Benjamin Hovland, later spoke publicly with NPR about the dismissal — a rare on-record account from inside a commission that usually operates far from the spotlight. (This card describes the U.S. Election Assistance Commission specifically; election administration varies by country.)

related.title: Can the President Fire the Heads of Independent Agencies?
related.hook: For 91 years, a 1935 precedent shielded independent agency heads from being fired at a president's will. In 2026 the Supreme Court swept most of that shield away.

related.title: Who Can Vote: Suffrage
related.hook: Democracy means rule by the people — but for most of history, 'the people' meant a narrow few. The story of suffrage is the slow widening of that circle.

related.title: Accountability & Oversight
related.hook: Power left unwatched drifts toward abuse. Accountability is the demand that officials answer for what they do — and oversight is the machinery that makes them.

flashcards.prompt: What is the U.S. Election Assistance Commission, and why was it built to be bipartisan?
flashcards.back_html: A federal body created after the 2000 Florida recount to set voluntary voting-system standards and support local election officials. It's capped at no more than two commissioners from one party, so election administration isn't controlled by a single party.

flashcards.prompt: What happened to the EAC in July 2026?

choices.text: The president removed its remaining commissioners, leaving it without statutory leadership before the midterms
Congress voted to abolish it entirely
It was given direct authority to run state elections

flashcards.explanation_html: NPR and ProPublica both reported the president removed the commission's last sitting members, though the agency itself continues to exist.

flashcards.prompt: Who actually runs U.S. elections day-to-day?

choices.text: State and local election officials — the EAC only sets voluntary standards and offers support

flashcards.explanation_html: The EAC has no operational power over elections; the U.S. system is deliberately decentralized, run state by state.
